qa.name: Fibularis Longus
qa.origin: Upper two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula and lateral condyle of tibia
qa.insertion: Medial cuneiform and base of first metatarsal (plantar surface) — crosses the sole diagonally
qa.innervation: Superficial fibular (peroneal) nerve (L5, S1); longer tendon crosses sole
qa.function: Everts the foot; plantarflexes the ankle; supports the transverse and lateral longitudinal arches of the foot
qa.clinical_note: Fibularis Longus has the longest course of any fibular muscle — its tendon wraps behind the lateral malleolus, under the foot, and crosses diagonally to insert on the medial side. This diagonal course makes it a key supporter of the transverse arch. The superficial fibular nerve (L5–S1) innervates both fibularis longus and brevis — injury at the fibular neck (e.g. from a knee varus stress, fibular neck fracture, or prolonged squatting) causes eversion weakness and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Fibularis longus and tibialis anterior form a stirrup supporting the medial and lateral arches.

qa.name: Fibularis Brevis
qa.origin: Lower two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula
qa.insertion: Tuberosity (styloid process) at the base of the fifth metatarsal
qa.innervation: Superficial fibular (peroneal) nerve (L5, S1); inserts on 5th metatarsal base
qa.function: Everts the foot; plantarflexes the ankle; stabilises the lateral ankle
qa.clinical_note: Fibularis Brevis inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal — an avulsion fracture here (dancer's fracture) is the most common foot fracture, caused by forced inversion when fibularis brevis pulls off its bony attachment. This must be distinguished from a Jones fracture (transverse fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal) which has a higher nonunion rate. Both fibularis muscles share their nerve (superficial fibular, L5–S1) and travel posterior to the lateral malleolus in a shared synovial sheath.
